metadata.title: Oracle Plans More Layoffs as AI Spending Surges

content.text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is reportedly preparing another round of layoffs as the software giant tries to contain payroll costs while pouring tens of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure. Some teams could face double-digit percentage reductions, highlighting a growing investor tension: Oracle's cloud business is accelerating rapidly, but funding that growth is putting unprecedented pressure on capital spending, cash flow and the balance sheet.
Oracle sells enterprise databases, business applications and cloud infrastructure through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI. AI demand has increasingly shifted its growth engine toward cloud computing, where it competes with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Google (NASDAQ:GOOG).
Managers have reportedly been asked to identify employees for cuts ahead of Oracle's fiscal second quarter, which begins Sept. 1. The company's workforce has already fallen to roughly 141,000 employees from 162,000 a year earlier.
The cuts come despite booming demand. Fiscal 2026 revenue rose 17% to a record $67.4 billion, while cloud revenue surged 39% to $34 billion.
But infrastructure spending has risen even faster. Oracle spent roughly $42.7 billion on capital expenditures during fiscal 2026 as it raced to add data-center capacity. Earlier this year, the company outlined plans to raise $45 billion to $50 billion through debt and equity to support additional cloud infrastructure.
That makes the layoffs less a traditional response to weak demand and more an attempt to redirect resources toward Oracle's capital-intensive AI buildout.
Investor Takeaway On Oracle Stock
Investors should watch whether workforce reductions translate into better operating leverage without slowing cloud execution.
The critical metrics are OCI growth, capex, free cash flow, debt and the speed at which new AI data-center capacity converts into revenue. Strong cloud growth would make Oracle's aggressive spending easier to defend.
The risk is that infrastructure costs and borrowing continue rising faster than monetization. Oracle's AI strategy is producing exceptional demand, but repeated layoffs underscore the price management is willing to pay elsewhere in the business to fund it.
